P1.evidence: The setter handover was used specifically and early — 'Of course, I saw that you climb like two, four days a week' — and the prospect confirmed a prior conversation had happened. The frame covered where he is and where he wants to go plus the disqualification promise, but not what is in the way or what he needs. Agreement taken ('okay?' — 'Okay. Perfect.') and the open question asked cleanly.

P2.evidence: Work was the best-run check in the batch: 'And what sort of work do you do at the moment?' followed by a probe on whether it is sedentary, producing the 20-person team and the 60/40 split. Injuries were asked well and in a form tailored to the sport. Diet was mapped in detail including the workplace lunches. But age, height and current weight were never asked at all — his birth year entered the record only because a credit application asked for it at 00:51, and his body fat is recorded as his own guess with 'I don't actually know' attached. Sleep is the costly miss again: he wakes at 4am, starts work at 5.30 and has a newborn arriving in August, and it was never raised. Energy never asked.

P3.evidence: The strongest goals work in the batch. He forced the vague ambition into something measurable — 'you want to get into a tremendous shape. But just explain to me what that is' — which produced the strength-to-weight framing. The bridge was excellent and used the prospect's own comparative position: 'So many people are like in more of a management position, already working out like two, four days a week with climb, and they're like, I would sign for this... So why is it important for you to not stay at that level?' The drive-through reached fatherhood, legacy and identity without being forced, and the reflect-back was delivered twice, including 'It sounds like the weight isn't really the most important. It comes down to that ratio between strength and weight.' Only P3c is soft — the goal peaks were surfaced as aspiration rather than as capability he currently lacks.

P4.evidence: 'You've never had a coach before. One reason was because you always just want to prove to yourself that you can do it without having that outside accountability' correctly read back the history, and 'for how long have you had the idea that you are in okay shape, but you want to get better?' dated the plateau at eight or nine months. He let the prospect name the gap himself — structure, routine and a sounding board. Two softer points: the why-it-didn't-stick question was never asked directly, and 'what are things that you would need from him?' is forward-looking rather than diagnostic. The information-isn't-the-problem line never ran, though it matters less here because the prospect never claimed information was the issue.

P5.evidence: The two-year picture was never asked. There is no point in this call where the prospect is made to describe what happens if nothing changes, which on a man about to have a second child is the most available material on the table. The only settle-adjacent moment is a reflection rather than a question — 'You don't want to settle for what you currently have', answered 'I don't want to settle.' No why-not and no line in the sand. The consequence of the omission shows up at the price: the prospect's own stated stake never rose above wanting more, so when the funding failed there was nothing pressing him to solve it.

P6.evidence: The belief question ran twice and was properly framed around sustaining it after the engagement ends: 'do you feel like if we basically dial in on those three things, you're actually going to be able to stick to that and not give up on it when you stop working with us?' returned 'Yeah. No, I definitely think that.' The gate was clean and unconditional — 'this is something I see myself going through' and 'I definitely see myself going through it' — before any number was named. The all-in question was never asked in its scripted form.

P11.evidence: Step 2 was executed properly and completely: Trevor's onboarding call was booked for Wednesday 4.15pm Pacific and the invite was confirmed received on the call. Step 1 was not — $100 of $6,000 was collected and the balance has no funding path. The order is also inverted against the rule the manager gave this rep, and against the rep's own stated understanding: 'I cannot book in a meeting until, like, there's some sort of form of commitment.' Nothing was said about the agreement email or signing it, and nothing about the welcome email, the Skool link or the onboarding questionnaire.

objection_plays.detail: On paper this looks like the fullest money play in the batch, and in substance it is the play being replaced by lender troubleshooting. What ran: the isolate, cleanly; the open-conversation ask, near verbatim — 'Luckily, we're not as firm as like, you can only do it in that way. So if you want, we can talk about it, see if we can figure something out'; the most-clients-pay-upfront line — 'Most guys always just put it upfront on their credit card because it also locks in their accountability'; and, unusually, four financial-picture items — number of cards ('It's my only one'), limit ('What's the limit? 2k'), used versus available ('do you think that the usual charges are per month... 500 to 600') and a monthly maximum. But those four emerged as debugging output from a declined credit application, not from an open financial conversation, and the two that were never asked are the two that might have funded it: savings and investments. The prospect volunteered a savings hypothetical — 'hey, actually, I got more in my savings than I thought' — and it was not picked up. Thirty minutes went into making a lender pay rather than finding where the prospect's own money is.

'And this is something obviously I'd have to talk with my partner about as well' at 00:47:42. Not one move ran, and the subject was never raised again across the remaining thirty-seven minutes, through three financing attempts, a $100 payment and the booking of an onboarding call. The play was unusually available here: the partner is seven weeks from giving birth, they have a shared and still-outstanding $6,000 midwife obligation, and the whole emotional case the rep had already built was about being the father his son needs — 'is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger' writes itself.

Financing declined live. There is no scripted path for what happens when the funding mechanism itself fails — twice, across two providers, in front of the prospect. The improvisation was a $100 holding payment, an onboarding booking taken on the strength of it, and homework for the prospect to get his credit union to raise his card limit. This is a genuine gap in the script rather than a rep failure, and it is worth the script owner's attention because the diagnosis was available in two minutes: a single card with a $2,000 limit cannot carry a $6,000 purchase whatever the credit score is.

notes: Phases 1, 3, 4 and 6 were the best work in this batch — the bridge question at 00:07:09 and the strength-to-weight reflect-back are worth using as training clips. Two things cost it. Phase 5 never ran, so a prospect who was already sold had no urgency to solve a funding problem for. And when the price landed, thirty minutes went into troubleshooting a lender instead of running the play: savings were never asked about, and the partner who was named as a required conversation was never returned to before money changed hands.
